analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal corporate income taxes, capital gains taxes, and the estate tax.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut the corporate tax rate to 0%, make capital gains tax-free, and repeal the estate tax was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on June 14, 2013 and never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal corporate income tax by setting the corporate rate and the corporate alternative minimum tax at 0%, and it would have made all net capital gains — profits from selling stocks and other investments — completely tax-free. It also would have repealed the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes outright and extended 100% "bonus depreciation" (immediate write-offs of business equipment purchases) for three years. The bill contained no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts to make up the lost revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporations are the biggest beneficiaries: they would pay zero federal income tax in every year after 2013. Wealthy households and investors gain enormously from the full exclusion of capital gains from income, and the heirs of the largest estates gain from the outright repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes. Businesses buying equipment gain from three more years of 100% bonus depreciation. Because most capital gains and taxable estates belong to households at the very top of the income distribution, the benefits are heavily concentrated there.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large corporations and the wealthiest households

how_it_helps.text: Would set the corporate income tax rate and the corporate alternative minimum tax rate at 0% for tax years beginning after 2013, ending federal corporate income taxes altogether.
Would exclude all net capital gain from taxable income, meaning profits from selling stocks, bonds, and other investments would never be taxed.
Would repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely for deaths and gifts after enactment, ending the only federal tax on inherited multimillion-dollar fortunes.
Would extend 100% bonus depreciation — the ability to write off the full cost of equipment purchases immediately — through the end of 2017 for businesses.

analysis.who_pays: The bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts, so the federal government would lose all corporate income tax revenue, all capital gains tax revenue, and all estate and gift tax revenue. Since capital gains and large taxable estates are concentrated among the highest-income households, the direct beneficiaries would be at the top while the lost revenue — hundreds of billions of dollars per year by any standard estimate — would have to be made up through more borrowing or through cuts or tax increases falling on everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary taxpayers, through deficits or service cuts

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no offsetting revenue: it eliminates corporate income taxes, capital gains taxes, and the estate tax without a single tax increase or spending cut to pay for them, so the cost would land on future budgets either as larger deficits or as cuts elsewhere.

The tax cuts are aimed where the money is concentrated: corporations pay the corporate tax, and capital gains and large taxable estates overwhelmingly belong to the wealthiest households, so the bill's benefits would flow mostly to those already at the top.

Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes entirely — rather than raising the exemption amounts, which Congress had already done — ends all federal taxation of the largest intergenerational wealth transfers, permanently if not later restored.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers no serious mechanism for paying for itself. Extending bonus depreciation for three years is a conventional, if expensive, business-investment incentive, but pairing it with a 0% corporate rate, a full capital gains exclusion, and total estate tax repeal — with zero offsets — would shift an enormous revenue burden onto everyone who does not earn income through corporate profits, investment gains, or inherited fortunes. As drafted, the costs to the broad public dwarf the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a markup or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun of Georgia introduced the bill on June 14, 2013, with six Republican colleagues signing on as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; that was the last action of any kind recorded on it.
No committee markup, floor vote, or any other action ever took place, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off than they would have been under the bill, since no revenue was stripped out of corporate, capital gains, and estate taxation without anything to replace it. The bill's sponsors and supporters failed to advance their proposal at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers avoided the tax cuts' cost

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the only recorded positions are the seven Republican sponsors and cosponsors; no member ever went on record for or against it.

industries.note: The bill would have set the corporate tax rate and corporate AMT at 0%, eliminating federal corporate income taxes entirely. Corporations' gain would come directly at the cost of the federal revenue that funds public services.

Excluding all net capital gains from income would have made investment profits — including fund managers' carried interest — completely tax-free. Because capital gains are concentrated among the wealthiest households, the gain and the public's cost are two sides of the same ledger.

Full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would let the largest fortunes pass to heirs with no federal tax at all. Only a small share of estates — the largest — currently owe any estate tax.

A three-year extension of 100% bonus depreciation would let any business buying equipment deduct the full cost immediately, improving cash flow. The benefit is broad but deficit-financed, since the bill provides no way to pay for it.
